name: Amminadab
title: Patriarch of the tribe of Judah and link in the messianic lineage
summary: Amminadab, son of Ram, was a central figure in the tribe of Judah who played an important role in Israel's family history. He was the father of Nahshon, who led the tribe of Judah during the wilderness journey, and the father of Elisheba, who according to Exodus 6:23 married the high priest Aaron. Through this marriage, a remarkable connection was established between the royal line of Judah and the priestly line of Levi – two lines that both point forward to the Messiah. Amminadab forms an important link in the unbroken genealogy from Judah to King David and onward to Jesus Christ, as shown in the genealogies in both the Old and New Testaments.
roles: father-in-law of the high priest Aaron

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the lineage of Judah
keyEvents.description: Amminadab is listed as the son of Ram and father of Nahshon in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah, and his son Nahshon is mentioned as leader of Judah.

keyEvents.title: Elisheba, Daughter of Amminadab, Marries Aaron
keyEvents.description: Amminadab's daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron, Israel's first high priest. The text identifies her as 'the daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon.' This marriage created an important connection between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Levi.

keyEvents.title: In the Genealogies of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Amminadab is mentioned in the detailed genealogy that connects Judah to David through an unbroken line via Perez, Hezron, and Ram.

keyEvents.title: In the Lineage of the Book of Ruth
keyEvents.description: Amminadab is listed in the genealogy at the end of the Book of Ruth, linking Perez to King David through ten generations.

keyEvents.title: In Matthew's Genealogy of Jesus
keyEvents.description: Amminadab is included in Matthew's genealogy showing Jesus' descent from Abraham through Judah's royal line.

keyEvents.title: In Luke's Genealogy of Jesus
keyEvents.description: Luke includes Amminadab in his lineage that traces back from Jesus through David and further to Adam and God.

versions.reason: [minor] Amminadab is not directly described as a 'leader' in the Bible. His son Nahshon was leader of the tribe of Judah. 'Patriarch' or 'forefather' would be more precise than 'leader'. The role of 'patriarch' can also be discussed, since this term is usually reserved for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.; [minor] According to traditional reading and some texts, Amminadab's daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron (Exod 6:23). Although his wife is not named in the Bible, it may be noted that he had a daughter (Elisheba). This is relevant family information that is missing.; [minor] In Exod 6:23, Elisheba is mentioned as the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon. She should be added as a child (elisjeba).; [minor] A key event linked to Exod 6:23 is missing, where Elisheba, Amminadab's daughter, is mentioned as Aaron's wife. This is an important link between the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Levi.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1500 BC' is approximately acceptable, but there are various chronologies. This is an important theological detail.; [minor] The last key event ('Nahshon's father and leader in Israel') overlaps strongly with the first event. footnotes.text: The name Amminadab (Hebrew: עַמִּינָדָב, 'Amminadav') means 'my people are noble' or 'my kinsman is generous.' The combination of 'ammi' (my people) and 'nadav' (to be noble, generous) reflects a pride in the tribe's honor, typical of Hebrew personal names from this period.

According to Exodus 6:23, Amminadab's daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron, Israel's first high priest, and became the mother of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. This marital alliance between the tribes of Judah and Levi created a unique connection between the royal and priestly lines in Israel—a motif with theological significance in light of the messianic expectation of a figure who unites the roles of king and priest.

In rabbinic tradition, Amminadab is a respected figure. According to the Talmud (Sota 37a), his son Nahshon was the first Israelite who, with faith and courage, stepped into the Red Sea. This tradition highlights the family's piety and leadership qualities, and is regarded by the rabbis as an example of faith in action.

Amminadab belongs to the fourth generation after Judah in the lineage: Judah → Perez → Hezron → Ram → Amminadab. The fact that the genealogies in 1 Chron 2:10, Ruth 4:19–20, Matt 1:4, and Luke 3:33 all agree on this placement underscores the biblical tradition's deliberate focus on an unbroken line of descent from the patriarchs to the Messiah.

It is worth noting that there appear to be very few generations between Judah and the time of Moses—only four links from Judah to Amminadab. Some scholars believe that the biblical genealogies may omit intermediate links and mention only the most prominent names, a known practice in Semitic lineage lists where 'son of' can also mean 'descendant of.'
